extracted.intended_audience: students, readers, and practitioners of art, architecture, and sculpture; art historians and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Critical evaluation and description of architectural sculpture and ornament (especially Gothic and Renaissance) as they function on buildings — placement, subject, execution, durability, and symbolic meaning, using the Ducal Palace at Venice as primary example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking the angle (Gothic principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This principle of breaking the angle is peculiarly Gothic' — sharp building angles should be modified by groups of buttresses, turrets, niches, or sculpture to soften and enrich them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as both structural necessity (strengthening flanks with buttresses/pinnacles) and aesthetic remedy for 'meagreness' where large wall surfaces meet; examples include buttresses, turrets, and the Ducal Palace's angle sculpture (gargoyle, projecting angels). Anti-pattern: leaving the angle unrelieved produces meagre effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the principal decoration on building angles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ducal Palace 'throws the main decoration upon its angles' — angles are used as the loci for important sculptural subjects and visual emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural arrangement described: enlarged pillars and capitals at angles, sculptural subjects above capitals (life-size figures in lower arcade; single angels in upper arcade), and twisted pillars with niches forming an unbroken vertical line of decoration from ground to top. Implication: important messages/themes are physically located at corners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corner sculptures must convey principal intent and sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'These... are the very corner stones of the edifice, and in them we may expect to find the most important evidences of the feeling, as well as of the skill, of the builder.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of subject at corners communicates the purpose or lesson the builder wished to teach — e.g., at the Ducal Palace: Fall of Man (Fig-tree angle), Drunkenness of Noah (Vine angle), Judgment of Solomon (Judgment angle). Use corner placement intentionally to state civic or spiritual temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject selection expresses school/spirit (Gothic vs Renaissance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection of subjects reveals 'the temper of the two schools' — Gothic works confess human frailty, Renaissance works show confidence in wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Ducal Palace: Gothic corners (Fall of Man, Drunkenness of Noah) vs Renaissance corner (Judgment of Solomon). Guidance: read subject-matter as ideological program; anti-pattern: treating subject choice as merely decorative without ideological reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism and fidelity in vegetal carving (leafage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic naturalism often attains greater success in leafage than in figures — 'Nothing can be more masterly... than the sweep of this foliage' and leaves may be carved with every rib and vein in relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High finish in leafage (deep undercutting, carved veins and ribs) produces powerful visual effect and durability when mass is strong. Example contrast: fig-tree leafage (nobler masses) vs vine (delicate tendrils prone to breakage). Anti-pattern: over-refining delicate parts where exposure will cause loss of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance finish/detail with material durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive delicacy (as in vine tendrils) can lead to breakage; strong, large masses survive better — 'the natural delicacy... tempted the sculptor to greater effort... half of them have been broken away.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When carving exposed architectural sculpture, consider the limits of the medium and site exposure: favor structural robustness for long-term survival. Use fine finish where protected or on robust forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures may be technically inferior to ornament yet still effective
rubrics_metrics.description: In early sculpture 'the figures are much inferior to the leafage; yet so skilful in many respects' — figures can lack finish compared to botanical carving but still convey power or intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge a sculpture solely by anatomical finish; consider overall composition, stylistic intent, and relationship to surrounding ornament. Example: figures on Ducal Palace are stiff but appropriate for architectural service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale, placement, and legibility relative to viewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals and sculptures positioned about eight feet above the eye were intended 'to be read, like the pages of a book' by those who walked beneath — scale and height determine legibility and narrative function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sculptural narratives for the expected viewer distance and angle; elements intended for close reading should be placed lower or exaggerated in scale. Anti-pattern: fine-detailed, small-scale work placed where it cannot be visually read by intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personification versus symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification (giving human form to abstract ideas) is generally the lighter, less noble mode; symbolism (using imperfect signs to suggest a great truth) is more solemn and spiritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personification suits decorative or imaginative purposes but can 'disturb the belief in the reality' of what is personified; symbolism is preferred in serious religious moods. Historical note: increase in personification marks decline in spiritual vitality in the Church's art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and classification of virtues in art reflect theological/intellectual tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The number, nature, and ordering of depicted virtues vary with the artist's aim and the intellectual climate; later periods tended to classify virtues into enumerated systems (cardinal/theological), sometimes confusing duties with virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the depiction of virtues may follow scholastic/classical schemes (e.g., adding Faith, Hope, Charity to the four cardinals) and that such systematization can produce mechanical personifications. Example: Giotto arranges virtues differently for different settings (Assisi vs Arena Chapel). Anti-pattern: rigid, pedantic lists that obscure spiritual meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification quality depends on spiritual sincerity of the artist
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In the hands of its early and earnest masters, personification is... thoroughly noble and lovely; the earlier conditions of it being... more spiritual and vital.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess personification by the depth and sincerity behind it — noble personification arises from genuine faith or earnestness; shallow personification signals mere fancy or formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of decorative motif with structural form
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorative elements (e.g., tree trunks, serpents) should act as 'terminal group of lines' that harmonize with the building's geometry — the trunk of the tree forms the true outer angle of the palace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose ornament so that its major forms serve structural/architectural purposes (masking corners, completing lines, creating continuity) rather than appearing as applied afterthoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical continuity of ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Twisted pillars with crowning niches form 'an unbroken line of decoration from the ground to the top of the angle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vertical sequences (capitals, figures, spiral shafts, niches) to create coherent upward movement and unify multi-story façades. Avoid disjointed or scattered ornament that fails to lead the eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptural motifs should reinforce moral or civic messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Angels and small attendant figures (e.g., Tobit with Raphael) 'express... the consciousness of human frailty, and the dependence upon Divine guidance' — sculptural programs serve didactic functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose motifs and attendant details to reinforce the building's intended message (religious, civic, moral). Example: small figure touching hem of Raphael to express dependence; anti-pattern: decorative figures that contradict or dilute the intended message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic details can date works and indicate influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of dress or execution (e.g., bandaged feet in figure sculpture) serve as stylistic markers for dating ('a feature... found in nearly every piece of figure sculpture in Venice, from the year 1300 to 1380').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent stylistic elements—costume, hair treatment, carving technique—to place works in time and to infer workshop influence; cross-reference with dated monuments and inscriptions.
